question: At what height above a lower level does OSHA require fall protection for construction workers on an unprotected side or edge?
answer: OSHA requires fall protection for each employee on a walking/working surface with an unprotected side or edge which is 6 feet or more above a lower level [1926-subpart-M | 1926.501]. Employers must protect workers using guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall arrest systems [1926-subpart-M | 1926.501].

question: What roof slope counts as a steep roof?
answer: A steep roof is defined as a roof having a slope greater than 4 in 12 (vertical to horizontal) [1926-subpart-M | 1926.500].

question: How high must the top rail of a guardrail system be above the walking surface?
answer: The top edge height of top rails for standard guardrail systems must be 42 inches plus or minus 3 inches above the walking or working level, though the height may exceed 45 inches when conditions warrant provided the system meets all other criteria [1926-subpart-M | 1926.502]. When employees are using stilts, the top rail height must be increased by an amount equal to the height of the stilts [1926-subpart-M | 1926.502]. For scaffolds, different height requirements apply depending on when the scaffold was placed in service and the type of scaffold [1926-subpart-L | 1926.451].

question: What is the most force a personal fall arrest system may put on a worker wearing a body harness when it stops a fall?
answer: When stopping a fall, a personal fall arrest system must limit the maximum arresting force on an employee to 1,800 pounds (8 kN) when used with a body harness [1926-subpart-M | 1926.502].

question: How far below the working surface can a safety net be installed at the most?
answer: Safety nets must be installed as close as practicable under the walking/working surface, but in no case more than 30 feet (9.1 m) below that level [1926-subpart-M | 1926.502].

question: How much weight must an anchorage for personal fall arrest equipment be able to support?
answer: Anchorages used for the attachment of personal fall arrest equipment must be capable of supporting at least 5,000 pounds (22.2 kN) per employee attached, or else be designed, installed, and used under qualified supervision as part of a complete system that maintains a safety factor of at least two [1926-subpart-M | 1926.502]. Additionally, these anchorages must be independent of any anchorage being used to support or suspend platforms [1926-subpart-M | 1926.502].

question: What must the written certification of fall protection training contain?
answer: The written certification record of fall protection training must contain the name or other identity of the employee trained, the date or dates of the training, and the signature of the person who conducted the training or the signature of the employer [1926-subpart-M | 1926.503]. If the employer relies on training conducted by another employer or completed prior to the effective date of the section, the record must indicate the date the employer determined the prior training was adequate instead of the date of actual training [1926-subpart-M | 1926.503].

question: How deep must a trench be before a ladder, stairway or ramp for getting out is required, and how close to workers must it be?
answer: A stairway, ladder, ramp, or other safe means of egress must be located in trench excavations that are 4 feet (1.22 m) or more in depth [1926-subpart-P | 1926.651]. It must be placed so that it requires no more than 25 feet (7.62 m) of lateral travel for employees [1926-subpart-P | 1926.651].

question: How far from the edge of an excavation must dug-out soil and equipment be kept?

question: When does an excavation not need a protective system against cave-ins?
answer: An excavation does not need a protective system against cave-ins when the excavation is made entirely in stable rock [1926-subpart-P | 1926.652]. It is also exempt when the excavation is less than 5 feet in depth and an examination of the ground by a competent person provides no indication of a potential cave-in [1926-subpart-P | 1926.652].

question: What is the maximum allowable slope for Type C soil?

question: How wide may the gap between scaffold platform units be?

When a wider space is necessary, the open space between the platform and the uprights must not exceed 9 1/2 inches (24.1 cm) [1926-subpart-L | 1926.451].

question: When does a scaffold have to be inspected, and by whom?
answer: Scaffolds and scaffold components must be inspected for visible defects by a competent person before each work shift, and after any occurrence that could affect the structural integrity of the scaffold [1926-subpart-L | 1926.451].

question: How close may a scaffold get to an insulated power line carrying less than 300 volts?

question: How far must a portable ladder extend above the upper landing it is used to reach?
answer:
When portable ladders are used for access to an upper landing surface, the ladder side rails must extend at least 3 feet above the upper landing surface [1926-subpart-X | 1926.1053]. 

When such an extension is not possible because of the ladder's length, the ladder must be secured at its top to a rigid support that will not deflect, and a grasping device such as a grabrail must be provided to assist employees in mounting and dismounting [1926-subpart-X | 1926.1053]. In no case shall the extension be such that ladder deflection under a load would, by itself, cause the ladder to slip off its support [1926-subpart-X | 1926.1053].

question: When is a stairway or ladder required at a point of access on a construction site?
answer: A stairway or ladder must be provided at all personnel points of access where there is a break in elevation of 19 inches (48 cm) or more, provided that no ramp, runway, sloped embankment, or personnel hoist is provided [1926-subpart-X | 1926.1051].

question: At what angle should a non-self-supporting ladder be set up?
answer: Non-self-supporting ladders shall be used at an angle such that the horizontal distance from the top support to the foot of the ladder is approximately one-quarter of the working length of the ladder, which is the distance along the ladder between the foot and the top support [1926-subpart-X | 1926.1053]. Additionally, wood job-made ladders with spliced side rails shall be used at an angle such that the horizontal distance is one-eighth the working length of the ladder [1926-subpart-X | 1926.1053].

question: What head protection is required where there is a danger of head injury from falling objects?
answer: Employees working in areas where there is a possible danger of head injury from falling or flying objects must be protected by protective helmets [1926-subpart-E | 1926.100]. When an employee is exposed to falling objects, the employer shall have each employee wear a hard hat and implement specific measures such as toeboards, screens, guardrail systems, canopy structures, or barricades [1926-subpart-M | 1926.501].

question: When may concrete forms and shores be removed?
answer:
Forms and shores, except those used for slabs on grade and slip forms, may be removed only after the employer determines that the concrete has gained sufficient strength to support its weight and superimposed loads [1926-subpart-Q | 1926.703]. 

This determination must be based on compliance with one of the following conditions:
- The plans and specifications stipulate conditions for removal of forms and shores, and those conditions have been followed [1926-subpart-Q | 1926.703].
- The concrete has been properly tested with an appropriate ASTM standard test method designed to indicate concrete compressive strength, and the test results indicate that the concrete has gained sufficient strength to support its weight and superimposed loads [1926-subpart-Q | 1926.703].
judge_reason: The answer accurately captures all the key facts, conditions, and exceptions for removing concrete forms and shores as stated in the evidence.

question: How large must the limited access zone be when a masonry wall is being built?

question: What must be done with protruding reinforcing steel that workers could fall onto?

question: How often must a competent person inspect an excavation?

question: Which temporary power outlets on a construction site need ground-fault circuit interrupters?
answer: All 120-volt, single-phase, 15- and 20-ampere receptacle outlets on construction sites that are not part of the permanent wiring of the building or structure and are in use by employees must have approved ground-fault circuit interrupters for personnel protection, unless an assured equipment grounding conductor program is used instead [1926-subpart-K | 1926.404]. An exception is made for receptacles on a two-wire, single-phase portable or vehicle-mounted generator rated at not more than 5kW, where the circuit conductors of the generator are insulated from the generator frame and all other grounded surfaces [1926-subpart-K | 1926.404].

question: Can a worker be allowed to work close enough to an electric power circuit to touch it?

question: A crew is working on a low-slope roof 20 feet up. Which fall protection options are allowed, and how far from the roof edge must a warning line be when no mechanical equipment is in use?

When no mechanical equipment is in use, the warning line must be erected not less than 6 feet from the roof edge [1926-subpart-M | 1926.502].

question: Workers on a scaffold 15 feet above the ground need what fall protection, and what training must they have had?

Employers must have each employee who performs work on a scaffold trained by a qualified person to recognize the associated hazards (including electrical, fall, and falling object hazards) and understand the procedures to control or minimize them [1926-subpart-L | 1926.454].
